claim: Deep knowledge tracing's headline lead over Bayesian knowledge tracing (AUC 0.86 vs 0.67-0.69 on ASSISTments) was mostly an artefact: about 31.6% of the gap came from a biased AUC procedure for BKT, another 50.6% vanished when BKT got forgetting (BKT 0.73, BKT+F 0.83).
agent_test: When comparing two reasoning scaffolds, re-run the weaker baseline with the same cheap extras (recency, forgetting) and the same scoring rule at equal tokens before crediting depth or size.

claim: The ASSISTments 0.86 AUC also depended on duplicate rows (about 25% of rows) that leak labels; removing them negated the gain, and hierarchical IRT matched or beat DKT on three datasets.
agent_test: Audit our own bench for duplicate or leaked items between scaffold tuning and test; report score with and without suspected leaks.

claim: Extended BKT is on average indistinguishable from DKT across four datasets (+20.0% Synthetic, +3.0% Spanish, -8.3% ASSISTments, -3.5% Statics); a logistic regression with good features leads DKT on 4 of 9 real datasets and DKT's edge is largest on big, sequence-rich data (assistments17 +0.056 AUC).
agent_test: For a per-skill competence tracker in the agent, compare a 3-feature logistic model (success count, failure count, recency) to a learned sequence model on logged agent runs at equal token cost.
audit_note: Edge on assistments17 is partly due to consecutive-attempt data (gap falls to +0.016 on first attempts).

claim: Benchmark inflation is common in knowledge tracing: label leakage from multi-concept questions adds a mean 8.38% (AS2009) and 13.09% (AL2005) AUC, ATKT's published results fail once future labels are removed, and newer models mostly do not clearly beat original DKT (AKT best by +0.3% to +3.06%). Leakage is dataset-specific: under 1 AUC point on single-skill sets (BD2006, NIPS34).
agent_test: Check that no scaffold step sees the gold answer or future steps; replay with leakage removed and compare.

claim: Zero-shot LLMs are poor at predicting whether a specific student answers the next item correctly: AUC 0.512-0.559 on FoundationalASSIST (baseline 51.3% accuracy, always-correct), 0.69 for Llama-3 8B zero-shot on ASSISTments, and accuracy below or near per-question baselines in the Eedi benchmark.
agent_test: Do not let the agent self-estimate user/task mastery by prompting alone; compare a prompted estimate with a count-based tracker on held-out logged outcomes.

claim: LLMs show strong optimistic bias when judging learners: Llama-3.3-70B was right 85.4% of the time when the student was correct but 12.6% when wrong; zero-shot Llama 3 8B recall on incorrect answers was only 20%. The bias is model-specific (Qwen3-80B-Instruct 56.5% vs 51.0%); fine-tuning raised low-performer recall from 20% to 64% but AUC stays below DKT (0.77 vs 0.83), and the zero-shot model's Youden-optimal threshold (0.8789 vs 0.5782 for DKT) shows its probabilities are inflated.
agent_test: Measure the agent's recall on its own wrong intermediate answers (self-check detecting errors) versus on right ones; correct for the optimism with a threshold or a separate verifier.
audit_note: Hooshyar et al. report 0.8789 vs 0.5782 only as Youden-optimal ROC thresholds used for sequence analysis; they do not show that raising the threshold reduces the optimism bias.
claim_before_audit: LLMs show strong optimistic bias when judging learners: Llama-3.3-70B was right 85.4% of the time when the student was correct but 12.6% when wrong; zero-shot recall on incorrect answers was only 20%. The bias is model-specific (Qwen3-80B-Instruct 56.5% vs 51.0%) and a higher decision threshold (0.8789 vs 0.5782 for DKT) or fine-tuning (low-performer recall 20% to 64%) reduces it, but AUC stays weak.

claim: Fine-tuning an LLM on interaction histories written as text beats ID-based KT when item text is used: NTKT LLaMA 3B AUC 90.32 vs DKT 72.37 on Eedi (ID-only 77.06, tags 84.59, full text 90.32); CLST gains up to 24.52% AUC with 8-64 students. But elsewhere the gain is small or negative (LKT: tie on XES3G5M-T, loss on small DBE-KT22; Hooshyar: fine-tuned 0.77 vs DKT 0.83; Eedi benchmark: specialised models 72.7-72.8% vs LLMs 58.6-66.5%). No independent replication of NTKT or CIKT found (gap 4 open); NTKT baselines omit any per-question or logistic-with-recency model.
agent_test: Not applicable to training; for scaffolds, test whether including item text in the tracker prompt beats IDs/tags only at equal tokens.

claim: Question text is where LLM-based tracing gets its edge: removing question information costs 3.08 AUC points on Nips2020 (LLM-KT, 0.8291 vs 0.7983; about 0.8 points on Assist2009), NTKT on Eedi rises from 77.06 AUC with IDs only to 90.32 with full question text, and text-based tracers (LKT) pre-trained on one dataset transfer to a new dataset without training while ID-based DKT drops to 0.5.
agent_test: Ablate task text versus task id in any retrieved-experience memory at equal tokens.
audit_note: In LLM-KT's ablation (Table 3) the 3.08-point AUC cost of removing question information (0.8291 vs 0.7983) is on Nips2020, not Assist2009 (where it is 0.8870 vs 0.8788, about 0.8 points).
claim_before_audit: Question text is where LLM-based tracing gets its edge: removing question information costs 3.08 AUC points on Assist2009 (LLM-KT), and text-based tracers transfer zero-shot to a new dataset while ID-based DKT drops to 0.5.

claim: A written, readable learner profile refined by feedback improves LLM prediction modestly: CIKT ACC 0.775/0.777 vs DKT 0.737, best classic 0.749, GPT-4o 0.732 on ASSIST2009; ablating profile, iteration or cooperation each lowers results and gains level off after about 3 rounds. Few-shot cognition-guided prompts matched full-data DKT on 2 of 3 datasets.
agent_test: Keep an agent-state profile (what it has verified, what is confused) rewritten each round up to 3 rounds; compare against no profile at equal tokens.

claim: In open tutoring dialogue, classic KT is near chance (BKT 52.50, DKT 53.20 AUC on CoMTA) while a fine-tuned LLM tracer with LLM-labelled knowledge components reaches 65.79 (CoMTA) and 76.71 (MathDial, 21x more data); GPT-4o labelling is near human but noisy.
agent_test: Label each turn of an agent run with knowledge components via an LLM and check whether the labels predict next-step success.

claim: A guarded, pedagogy-constrained LLM tutor can raise learning, while unrestricted help harms it: Kestin et al. N=194, median post 4.5 vs 3.5, effect 0.63 (regression), 0.73-1.3 SD (quantile); Bastani et al. about 1,000 students, GPT Base practice +48% but exam -17%, guarded GPT Tutor practice +127% with the harm largely removed. Correction: Bastani's GPT Tutor removed the harm but gave no positive unaided-exam effect. Lehmann et al. (Python, N=107 and 69 labs, 113-student field study) find no overall effect; harm comes from substitution use.
agent_test: Compare an agent that gets direct answers from a helper tool with one forced to produce its own step first (hints only), scored on a later no-helper run.

claim: LLM-generated hints can lose to human hints: ChatGPT hints gave 11.14% vs 24.63% gain (Elementary) and 1.7% vs 23.65% (Intermediate) in N=77; 30% of hints failed manual check. Single early test, older model.
agent_test: Gate generated hints/plans by a quality check before use and measure the share rejected.

claim: Real-time LLM support for human tutors raised mastery: +4 points exit-ticket pass (62% to 66%, p<.01), +9 points for lower-rated tutors, about 20 USD per tutor per year (700+ tutors, 1,000+ students).
agent_test: Assist-the-weaker-component pattern: give a hint-generating helper to the weaker solver mode and see whether the gain concentrates there.

claim: Step-based intelligent tutors are about as effective as human tutors: VanLehn (2011) human d=0.79 vs ITS d=0.76 (folk beliefs 2.0 and 1.0 not confirmed); Ma et al. (2014, 107 effect sizes, 14,321 learners) ITS vs individual human tutor g=-0.11; Kulik & Fletcher (2016) median +0.66 SD over 50 evaluations, strongly test-dependent. Field effects are smaller and delayed: Pane et al. (2014) none in year 1, +0.21 SD for high school in year 2 (middle school not significant); K-12 maths meta-analysis g=0.01-0.09; 2026 K-12 meta-analysis g=0.274. VanLehn's answer-based value (recalled 0.31) is still unverified. All from abstracts.
agent_test: Compare step-level checking against answer-only checking of a reasoning chain at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 0 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Adding faded worked examples to a Cognitive Tutor: adaptive fading beat fixed fading beat plain tutoring (Salden et al. 2010 abstract); a different study (Booth et al. 2013) found equal posttest and delayed scores but less learning time. Schwonke et al. (2009) exact numbers could NOT be obtained (paywalled). Evidence b28 pointed to a wrong DOI; the right one is 10.1016/j.chb.2008.12.011.
agent_test: Fade worked examples in the prompt as the tracker rises; measure tokens per correct answer.

claim: BKT is identifiable under mild conditions (Doroudi & Brunskill 2017), so the old 'non-identifiable' claim is wrong. The real risk is semantic degeneracy: when learners follow a different model, best-fit parameters contradict mastery and change with sequence length (e.g. fit says a master answers correctly 56% of the time vs true 90%, so the tutor stops practice too early). In a well-specified synthetic test (own simulation), near-best fits shift the 0.95 pass point by about one attempt, and 74% of them pass a C,C,I,C,C window. The 0.95 threshold is a convention.
agent_test: Sweep the agent's stop/mastery threshold, require a margin or two clean runs, and compare a fitted tracker against a simple count rule when the true learning curve is not two-state.

claim: LLMs judge relative item difficulty well (up to 68.6%, 80.0% on large gaps) but fall below chance on discrimination (best 46.9%) and rare distractors; explicit thinking helps abstract judgment but hurt concrete prediction (distractor 20.5%).
agent_test: Use the model for task difficulty ordering (cheap) but not for predicting which wrong answer it will produce.

claim: LLM tracers cost far more compute than KT models: DKT/SAKT under 0.25 s per student, GPT-4o-mini 3.1 s, Gemini 128 s, Qwen2.5-7B 3,299 s; authors report a 600-12,000x cost gap.
agent_test: Account for tracker tokens in the budget; prefer a count-based tracker unless the LLM version wins at equal tokens.

claim: Simulated students need explicit knowledge-state profiles: GPT-4 with mastered/confused/unknown profiles correlated r=0.72 with real students on per-question means (45 simulated vs 100 real, 20 MCQs) but failed when the right answer was unknown and a confused rule was available.
agent_test: Use profile-conditioned LLM simulations only to pre-screen items, then confirm on real logs.

claim: Item difficulty carries most of the predictable signal: a per-question average-correctness baseline gets 66.5% accuracy on Eedi, against 71.8% for DKT and 72.8% for an LLM tracer; several LLMs fall below it.
agent_test: Compare a count-based tracker (per task type) against any LLM-based self-estimate at equal tokens.

claim: No study yet compares an LLM tracer with a per-student logistic model with recency features on the same split; NTKT used only DKT, AKT, AKT-text and DTransformer as baselines.
agent_test: Run PFA/recency logistic vs the agent's text-based self-estimate on one split.

claim: No independent replication of NTKT (AUC 90.32) or CIKT was found; independent 2025-26 benchmarks (Worden, Hooshyar, Bhattacharyya) do not include them, and CIKT reports an 8:1:1 split with no leakage audit.
agent_test: Treat large LLM-tracer gains as unreplicated; re-run on a held-out split before use.

claim: Label noise in dialogue tracing is large but its cost is unmeasured: GPT-4o final-turn correctness accuracy 75.82% (83.33% on the human sample) vs 85.56% for teachers, with over 90% of labels correct.
agent_test: Track precision and recall on 'wrong' labels separately for the agent's own step labels.

claim: Effects of AI help depend on how it is used and on prior skill: asking for solutions speeds coverage but lowers understanding, asking for explanations raises it, and low-prior-knowledge learners lose most (Lehmann et al.); a scaffolded LLM beat plain ChatGPT in two experiments with delayed follow-up (ChatTutor), and a scaffolded LLM beat parent-led reading in a 67-child RCT with delayed tests. Meta-analyses of ChatGPT give g about 0.57 but mostly from assisted or immediate tests.
agent_test: Score unaided and delayed, split by agent skill level, and log whether help was a solution or an explanation.

claim: Gaps left open after search: (1) a tracker for an agent's own sub-skills improving routing or stopping at equal tokens has no direct study; (5) Schwonke 2009 numbers; (6) Pane per-level effect sizes and VanLehn answer-based d; (4) independent replication of NTKT/CIKT; noise cost in dialogue tracing.
agent_test: Run the agent-level tracker test directly: count-based tracker vs none at equal tokens.
